title: Is your game juicy enough? (summary of Jonasson & Purho, Juice it or lose it)
label: developer
claim: Juice = maximum output for minimum input; demo is a Breakout clone made lively by tweening, squash/stretch, sound; they claim graphics matter less than responsiveness. Secondhand summary, no data; presenters' opinion.

title: Indies resist the urge to juice it or lose it (Folmer Kelly counter-talk, GDC Europe)
label: snippet
claim: Counter-talk: polish makes a game feel alive but players may lose immersion; juice is not free.

title: How does juicy game feedback motivate? Testing curiosity, competence, and effectance (Kao et al., CHI 2024)
label: research
claim: Preregistered, 1,699 participants, action RPG, 2x2+control. Success-dependent feedback enhanced all motives; amplification (bigger feedback) unexpectedly REDUCED them, possibly undermining sense of control; curiosity the strongest predictor of enjoyment and only predictor of playtime; uncertain success affords curiosity.

title: Game feel (Swink definition)
label: snippet
claim: Swink: real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasised by polish; six areas input, response, context, polish, metaphor, rules. Defined around an avatar under real-time control.

title: Animation and motion (web.dev) / WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
label: practitioner
claim: prefers-reduced-motion is a sufficient technique for WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA); advice that non-essential animation can default to reduced; offer pause controls. Motion triggered by interaction is the target.

title: Dreamlight Valley accessibility (screen shake and flash toggles)
label: practitioner

title: Playing to wait: a taxonomy of idle games (Alharthi et al., CHI 2018)
label: research

title: The recipe behind Cookie Clicker (Game Developer, author's own analysis)
label: opinion
claim: Every cookie, achievement, generator or upgrade comes with visual feedback; early game showers the player in feel-good moments, later rewards get scarcer and shift to accomplishment; info presented transparently (costs, income, stats). Author says it is analysis, not Orteil's intent; nothing on sound.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, full list
label: practitioner
claim: Intermediate: provide an option to turn off/hide background movement; Advanced: option to turn off/hide all non-interactive elements, avoid sudden unexpected movement; Basic: avoid flickering images and repetitive patterns; Basic: no essential information conveyed by sound alone; Intermediate: replicate significant sound info in text or visuals. No screen-shake guideline in the list.

title: Designing Game Feel. A Survey (Pichlmair & Johansen), full text via pdftotext
label: research
claim: Defines juice as 'excessive amounts of feedback in relation to user input', superfluous mechanically, whose goal is to make actions feel significant; warns juice-rich interaction makes it hard to learn which aspects have mechanical importance. Confirms Kao [36]: medium and high juiciness outperformed extreme and none on player experience, intrinsic motivation, play time and in-game performance. Screen shake described as communicating a significant event; Nijman and Jonasson & Purho cited for it but no numbers given.

title: Kao et al., How does juicy game feedback motivate? (CHI 2024), full PDF via pdftotext
label: research
claim: Preregistered n=1,699, 2x2+control (amplification, success-dependence, variability). Curiosity strongest enjoyment predictor and only playtime predictor; success dependency drove curiosity, effectance and competence; amplified feedback lowered effectance (-.19) and competence (-.43) vs standard; enjoyment did NOT predict playtime; no direct amplification effect on enjoyment or playtime. Playtime lowest 6.17 min standard, highest 10.18 min in a success-dependent amplified cell. Cites Kao 2020 as n=3,018 goldilocks effect. Authors tentatively link amplification to impeded sense of agency.

title: Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
label: practitioner
claim: '0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously'; attributed to Miller (1968) and Card et al. (1991).

title: Understanding SC 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (W3C, WCAG 2.2)
label: guideline
claim: SC text: web pages 'do not contain anything that flashes more than three times in any one second period' (so three is allowed), OR the flash is below the general and red flash thresholds. General flash = 'a pair of opposing changes in relative luminance of 10% or more of the maximum relative luminance (1.0)'; passes if no more than three general and/or three red flashes in any one-second period. Area clause: combined area of concurrent flashes no more than .006 steradians within any 10 degree visual field (about 25% of it). Red flash = any pair of opposing transitions involving a saturated red. ITU-R BT.1702 cited for the luminance definition (20 cd/m2 change, darker image below 160 cd/m2). Harding and Trace Center (PEAT) are listed only as related resources. Read via a fetch-summariser, so wording is the summariser's quoting of the page; the Understanding page does NOT contain a '341 cd/m2' figure (341 x 256 px block is the 10-degree reference). UPGRADES the 'no more than 3 flashes per second' community summary (practitioner/snippet) to guideline.

title: Kao et al. CHI 2024, How does juicy game feedback motivate? (PDF, local copy read via pdftotext)
label: research
claim: Primary source for the CHI 2024 paper; its related-work paragraph describes Kao 2020: 'in a large between-subjects online study (n=3,018), Kao found evidence for a goldilocks effect: juiciness significantly affected competence, autonomy, presence/immersion, as well as interest/enjoyment, playtime, and performance; however, medium and high juiciness conditions outperformed low and extreme juiciness across all these measures'. It labels the weak conditions 'low and extreme' where the 2020 abstract excerpt (search result) says 'None and Extreme'. The same paragraph calls the evidence base 'characterised by mixed results, high measurement and operationalisation variance, low statistical power, and exploratory effect searching'. Still no effect sizes for Kao 2020: the paper (Entertainment Computing, doi 10.1016/j.entcom.2020.100359) is paywalled (sciencedirect 403).

title: Kao 2020, The effects of juiciness in an action RPG (Entertainment Computing 34:100359), full PDF read
label: research
claim: Between-subjects online (Amazon Mechanical Turk, US only, paid $1.50), N=3,018 (1,555 male, 1,463 female, age 18-80, M=35.5), one Unity WebGL action RPG built at four identical-but-for-effects versions made by a professional effects artist: None, Medium, High, Extreme. Each version changed audio (melee, ranged, spells, enemy sounds), visual effects (same attacks plus screen shakes) and menu hover/click audio-visuals (120+ visual and 120+ audio effects); visual and audio were never varied separately; no haptic or mechanical change. Pilot of 119 video raters: effect level rated 1-10 as None 5.06, Medium 5.38, High 5.64, Extreme 6.08 (only about one point from None to Extreme; 'None' is mid-scale, not minimal); fit of sounds/visuals did not differ (p=.85, .13). Frame rates matched within ~1 fps. Result (Tukey HSD): Medium and High are never different from each other on any measure. Extreme < Medium and High on competence (p<.05), autonomy (p<.01/.05), presence (p<.05), interest/enjoyment (p<.001/.005), value/usefulness (p<.05; Extreme also < None), time played (p<.05/.01), character level (p<.005/.001), total attacks (p<.005, vs Medium only), monsters defeated (p<.01), total keyboard/mouse actions (p<.005). None < Medium and High on competence (p<.05), time played (p<.05/.01) and keyboard/mouse actions (p<.05); None was NOT significantly worse on autonomy, presence, enjoyment, intrinsic motivation or character level, so the abstract's 'None and Extreme decreased intrinsic motivation' is not what the results section shows (RQ2 summary: Extreme only). Effect sizes are tiny: partial eta-squared .003-.010 (competence .005, enjoyment .006, time played .006, character level .006, keyboard/mouse actions .010); omnibus MANOVA partial eta-squared .003-.004. Per-condition n and raw means are not reported in text (figures only). Authors' limits: one game genre (casual games may suit Extreme, chess or Foldit-like performance games less), desktop display only, the four levels are bundles not single features, players could not switch between versions, moderate juice may cost things not measured (e.g. learning about the game world); preferred per-feature and per-player tailoring as next work.

title: Vice: Cookie Clicker wasn't meant to be fun (Orteil/Thiennot interview)
label: developer
claim: Orteil (Thiennot) quotes via fetch-summariser: 'We just tapped into the core psychological appeal behind a lot of games: getting something done.'; 'for idle games it's as bare-bones as making a number go up.'; idle devs design 'more sophisticated systems than just a basic Skinner box'; 'it's very convenient to have this endless design space.' The summariser reported NO quote on player feedback, upgrades or rewards. So the 'Cookie Clicker reads as feedback on every cookie' claim still has only the fan analysis; this adds designer context on why the loop works, not on feedback design.

title: The Longing (waits-and-ends)
label: opinion
claim: The 400-day wait runs in real time with the game closed; the game gives little direction on what to do while waiting ('It's not clear what there is to do or where to go'). Player reaction: Reviewer 'couldn't stay away', found forced patience 'enigmatically compelling'; also says it runs 'out of content way, way too soon'.

title: The Longing (waits-and-ends)
label: opinion
claim: Countdown runs in real time even closed; certain in-home actions speed it up (the wait is the mechanic, with things to do that nudge it). Player reaction: Aggregated: pace called tedious by many; some felt the premise cruel if they cannot engage often; a Steam poster said the payoff felt pointless (single opinion, AI-summarised aggregator).

title: guidance (waits-and-ends)
label: practitioner
claim: A wait that fits the fiction (build time, travel) reads as acceptable; an arbitrary cap on play reads as a block. Framing the same numbers differently changed player feeling (WoW halved XP renamed 'normal' vs 'bonus'). Page gives no wording for a blocked tap. Player reaction: WoW: 'players felt rewarded instead of punished' once relabelled.

title: guidance (waits-and-ends)
label: opinion
claim: Monetised timers reframe neutral time as scarcity; a wait with nothing to sell is not that, but the framing risk is the same. Player reaction: (fetch returned 403; text via search snippet only)
